resources.title: Straughan Recognition (athefre Google Site), including the Three Sticker Tracking section
resources.author: Michael James Straughan (Athefre)
resources.level: advanced (CMLL recognition, tracking and prediction for solvers who already know full CMLL; the NMCLL and ACMLL parts are for pseudo-block users)
resources.summary: A long Google Sites article (HTTP 200, rendered with Playwright, about 27k characters) that defines 'Straughan recognition', a minimum-sticker recognition concept Straughan developed in April/May 2024. Core claim: four side stickers identify any CLL/CMLL case, with no U stickers needed. By default these are the two F-colour and two R-colour stickers (FLU, FUR, RFU, RUB on a solved cube). ZBLL needs 6 stickers, 1LLL 7, OLLCP 4+3, two-sided PLL 5 and L5C (42 method) 5. Three recognition types: Object (track pre-chosen stickers wherever they are; meant for tracking, prediction and one-looking, and used by most sheets), Position (check fixed positions; for impromptu recognition) and Opportunistic (a mix). Listed advantages: minimum stickers; good for tracking and prediction; the same patterns work for CLL, TCLL+ and TCLL-; works with pseudo blocks. Listed disadvantages: each alg has 4 patterns, so CLL/CMLL means 162 patterns; Object type is not meant for in-the-moment recognition. The Roux section says the same four-sticker system applies to CMLL and ACMLL. It also offers a Three Corner CMLL variant (position type: only the visible stickers of the UFL, UFR and UBR corners) and a 'Permute First' two-look sheet. Pseudo section: NMCLL options 1 and 2 for R, R' and R2 non-matching blocks (learn the one sticker that changes), plus CCMLL options for the 42 method. Three Sticker Tracking (the section the hub points to): treat the two-sticker corner as one 'overall sticker' and track only the other two, giving a 3-sticker system. The idea is credited to Liam Highducheck and @effperm, and the purple one-colour display to Ethan Hayes. Other sections: Fourth Sticker Deduction (use colour order to infer an unseen sticker), Three Sticker Deduction (from the distinct-sticker-puzzles idea), Angles (if a tracked sticker is out of view, use other stickers on U/F/R so no AUF is needed), Organization, Rules and Observations, and Pattern Reduction Thoughts. The rules: at least 3 corners and 3 side stickers, because of a 'doppelganger effect'. Pattern reduction: learn only the best quarter of the patterns, or infer the invisible U-sticker orientation to cut 162 patterns down to 42. The non-Roux parts (2x2 CLL/EG/TCLL/LS, ZBLL, PLL, early corner permutation, Kilominx/Megaminx) are out of scope for a Roux-only app. Linked Google Sheets (fetched as CSV): the CMLL sheet has tabs Info, 2H, OH, Two Look, U Sticker, OH Codes and AUF Table. Its 2H tab holds 162 distinct pattern codes such as 'RUBRFU-FURFLU' (the positions of the two R stickers and the two F stickers), each with an alg and pre-AUF. The sheet recolours itself when a user copies it and changes the colour cells. The Three Corner CMLL sheet has tabs O, S, AS, L, U, T, Pi, H and 'Conditional Recognition', a decision procedure that starts from UFR's two non-U stickers, checks UFL, then UBR, and names the two-corner swap. The Permute First two-look sheet does corner permutation first (R U R' U' R' F R F' or F R U R' U' F' with an AUF), then OCLL-style orientation.

resources.title: Fengyuan Lou's guide to Meyer (a Discord message reposted as a Pastebin guest paste)
resources.author: Fengyuan Lou (per the resources.rouxers.com link text); Pastebin guest paste titled with a Discord message URL, pasted 2026-07-14, 47 views
resources.level: intermediate to advanced (Roux solvers deciding how to solve 4x4 and up; assumes they know Yau, centres and edge pairing)
resources.summary: A short plain-text explainer (about 230 words; raw fetched with HTTP 200). It covers the following. Meyer is a big-cube method for Roux users. It is essentially Yau, except that after the first 2 centres you build the first block instead of the first 3 cross edges, which is 'the same as first cross edges but with the corners inserted'. Next you solve the last 4 centres as in Yau. Then you pair edges with only 2 open slots instead of 4, because the first-block corners must be preserved. Finally you do the Roux 3x3 stage with the first block already solved. Opinion: Meyer is worse than Yau (the author says they have their own views on that), but probably the best option if you really want Roux on big cubes. The author thinks about 95% of Roux users would do better to get good at another method for big cubes (Yau/Hoya/Redux). Technical note: M-slice edge pairing suits Meyer better than E-slice pairing. So people who already pair on M (rare) may try Meyer, but E-slice pairers (about 99.9%) probably should not relearn edge pairing on a different axis just for this. There are no algorithms, diagrams or parity handling. On the hub it sits next to Kian's Meyer 4x4 tutorial and Louis' parity CMLL sheet.

resources.title: Jayden McNeill's insight on gatekeeping information (a Discord message reposted as a Pastebin guest paste)
resources.author: Jayden McNeill (per the resources.rouxers.com link text); Pastebin guest paste titled with a Discord message URL, pasted 2026-08-22, 69 views
resources.summary: A short informal opinion piece (about 300 words; raw fetched with HTTP 200), listed on the hub under 'Speedsolving Advice'. The author writes as someone who arguably would have benefited from not sharing his FMC knowledge in 2022-2024. Strategic angle: hiding a technique can help if your goal is a record. But if your goal is to be as good as possible, outside perspectives help refine what you found. And if someone else independently discovers and shares the same thing, they will probably get the naming credit. Psychological angle: he believes people who gatekeep take a bigger mental hit, because their subconscious reads it as 'I can't get a legitimate record unless I use this hidden advantage'. He links this to cubers who quit within about 5 years of WCA competition after others use and surpass their resources. He says he has always been willing to share and is confident in winning on skill. The tone is casual and includes a harsh insult toward gatekeepers. There is no Roux-specific content.

Who gets credit and naming for techniques
Mindset, motivation and longevity in competitive cubing

resources.title: The old man lost his horse (Wikipedia)
resources.author: Wikipedia contributors; parable from the Huainanzi, chapter 18 (2nd century BC); the article's translation is from Claude Larre et al., Les grands traites du Huainan zi (1993)
resources.summary: A Wikipedia article (HTTP 200; rendered text and raw wikitext saved) on the Chinese parable 'Sai Weng shi ma, yan zhi fei fu' (the old man of the frontier lost his horse; who knows if it is not good fortune). The hub links its #Translation section under 'Competition Advice'. Sections: Translation (classical Chinese and an English rendering), Plot and statement, Potential origin / chengyu / proverbs, Reception, In popular culture, Literature, References. The story: a man's horse runs away and neighbours pity him; the father asks 'who knows if this is not good luck?'. The horse returns with fine horses; 'who knows if this is not bad luck?'. The son breaks his leg riding them; then an invasion kills nine in ten local men, but the son is spared. The moral is that fortune and misfortune turn into each other and cannot be foreseen, so meet events with equanimity (the article links this to Taoist wu wei). The article also covers parallels in the Tao Te Ching, the Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese versions, Western proverbs ('blessing in disguise') and retellings (Alan Watts, Richard Wiseman). A banner says the article needs style editing (August 2024). For cubers the takeaway is: don't judge a round by one bad or good single; stay even-keeled.
drills: Competition equanimity practice: after a bad or great single, reset with the same routine instead of reacting, and judge only after the average

resources.title: 6.46s Speedsolving average of 100 by UNO on Cubeast (Fahmi's 2H Roux ao100)
resources.author: Cubeast user 'UNO' (Fahmi, per the hub link text; account timezone Asia/Jakarta). Average shared 2022-01-08; solves recorded 2022-01-01 to 2022-01-08 on a MoYu AI (Weilong AI) smart cube
resources.level: elite reference (6.46 s ao100, 2H 3x3 Roux); useful to intermediate and advanced solvers as a split benchmark
resources.summary: The cbst.link short link redirects by JS to app.cubeast.com/public/share/<id>, a public share of one Cubeast 'Average' (an Angular SPA explored with Playwright; its JSON API responses were captured). Header tiles: average 6.46 s, best 5.10, worst 7.52, 100 solves, 45.45 average turns (STM), 7.039 TPS. Cubeast trims the average by discarding the 5 best and 5 worst. Tabs. 'Average statistics' has sub-tabs. Overview: a stacked bar chart of recognition (blue) versus execution (orange) per step, for Pickup / Left block / Right block / CMLL / LSE / Put-down. Steps (per-step averages): Left block rec 0 / exec 0.79 / 6.60 turns / 8.30 TPS. Right block rec 0.23 / exec 2.04 (2.28 s) / 15.75 turns / 7.70 TPS. CMLL rec 0.69 / exec 0.64 (1.34 s) / 10.13 turns / 15.71 TPS / 1% skipped. LSE rec 0.52 / exec 1.49 (2.01 s) / 13.04 turns / 8.74 TPS. Cases: 'available only to Premium users'. Stats: inspection 11.63 s, pickup 0, total recognition 1.46 s, total execution 4.97 s, solving 6.45 s, penalties 0, 0.01 steps skipped. TPS: a per-step bar chart. 'Solves': a paginated table (#, Time, Turns, TPS; 25 per page, 4 pages). 'Rules': custom rules (cube, keyboard/touch and stackmat timers allowed, get-ready disabled, unlimited inspection, no custom scrambles). Clicking a solve opens a detail view: time/turns/TPS tiles, method 'Roux', ruleset, scramble with a copy button (random-state, 22 moves), and a 3D cube replay. The replay shows the current step name, time 'x s / total', move 'n / N', and rewind/step/play/step/fast-forward controls. Sub-tabs: Overview, Steps (adds a Case column), Solution (per-step move strings with rotations and inferred slice moves, e.g. 'z' y R' S R' B L F'' for left block, then RB, CMLL and LSE lines, with a copy button), Stats and TPS. Underlying data per solve: every move with a millisecond timestamp ('R'[73] D2[255] ...'), both orientation-normalised and as raw face turns, and per-step recognition time, execution time, turn metrics (face/slice/quarter) and TPS. Also inspection time, penalties flags, device (driver 'moyu', model 'MoYu AI'), colour scheme and solution rotation. Cubeast models Roux as 4 steps, each defined by a state pattern: Left block = BL FL DL DBL DLF, either side ('(LR)'); Right block adds FR BR DR DFR DRB; CMLL adds U corners with AUF 'U'; LSE = solved. So LSE is not split into EO/EOLR/4c. Sample solve #25 (6.06 s, 52 STM): LB 0.54 s, RB 1.73 s (0.09 rec), CMLL 1.05 s (0.52 rec, 0.53 exec, 20.8 TPS), LSE 2.74 s (0.48 rec). Social: 268 views, 1 like, 1 comment ('Congrats!'). There are no filters or search: one average per share. Key observation: even at 6.46, CMLL recognition (0.69 s) is longer than CMLL execution (0.64 s), and total recognition is 23% of solve time.

resources.title: Roux | Cubing History
resources.author: Michael James Straughan (Athefre), CubingHistory.com
resources.level: all levels for the lore; the technique sections name intermediate and advanced tools (NMCLL, DFDB, EOLR, ACMLL, CMLLEO, OH table abuse)
resources.summary: A Docusaurus page (HTTP 200; rendered text plus the Markdown source from the GitHub repo) with an annotated history of the Roux method and 48 footnotes. Many footnotes link to archive.org copies of Gilles Roux's original site, SpeedSolving threads and Discord messages. Description: proposed by Gilles Roux in 2003; steps are a left 1x2x3 block, a right 1x2x3 block, upper-layer corners, and the last six edges. Origin (from a private conversation with Roux): his earlier method ended with M/U edge algs; through Petrus with OCLL/PLL ('Petrich') he wanted F2L-like block building with an M/U finish, so he left the M slice out of F2L. Proposal: Yahoo Groups, August 2003. Also: LSE strategy evolution on Roux's site; the CMLL acronym (proposed on the site, later removed); Gilles once unofficially 2nd in the world on the speedcubing.com leaderboard. Advancements, with inventors and dates: misoriented centres (Roux's site, 2004); non-matching blocks and NMCLL 1 (Roux, Dec 2004, table completed by Straughan, Oct 2006); Hyperorientations (Robert Smith, 2007); NMCLL 2 (Straughan, Apr 2010); ATCRM (Straughan and Tim Mosher, Dec 2021); Straughan four-sticker recognition (2024). 4c recognition: FUBU (Straughan, Apr 2010, video by Michal Ciebiada); BU (popularised by Alex Lau); DFDB (Straughan, 2012, video by Bryan Rusinque; Yuta Sasaki's 2013 method to predict M2-start 3-cycles). CMLLEO (Thom Barlow, about 2010, first called KCLL). Table abuse for OH slice turns (Barlow, about 2010). EOLR/EOLRb (Straughan, Aug 2012; EOLR re-developed by Iuri Grangeiro with Kian Mansour, Aug 2016, and popularised by Kian). Pinkie Pie (Rob Stuart, Oct 2011; named by Alexander Lau, 2012). ACMLL (Straughan, proposed Apr 2020, presented Jan 2021). CMLL prediction (Zhouheng Sun's Nov 2020 NMCMLL-for-prediction idea; ATCRM and Straughan as candidates). Corner-orientation prediction (Straughan, Jul 2022: track corners during the last SB pair). The page embeds 2 YouTube videos (LKXdVfNaLao, Rusinque's 4b-to-4c; vW0bBDdoPlk), many screenshot exhibits and a solved-state cube Exhibit. Footer: 'Copyright (c) 2026 Michael James Straughan'. Source repo: github.com/mjstraughan/CubingHistory. The GitHub page was 403 via the proxy and the GitHub API is not enabled for this session. Raw README and package.json were readable; there is no LICENSE file and no licence field.

resources.summary: GitHub's generic how-to page. The old URL now redirects to /en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/creating-a-pull-request (HTTP 200). It is linked from the resources.rouxers.com Contributing page, which says the hub is hosted on GitHub (rouxers/resources, Hugo Book theme) and takes new resources by pull request or the per-page 'Edit this page' button. Content: anyone with read access can create a PR; fork first if you lack write access; PRs only go between two different branches; you can link a PR to an issue so it closes on merge. Creating: pick the branch, use 'Compare & pull request', choose the base and compare branches, add a title and description, then create a ready-for-review or draft PR. After opening, push more commits or edit files on the web from 'Files changed'. There are tool tabs for GitHub CLI, web browser, Desktop and Codespaces, plus further-reading links (PR from a fork, keeping in sync, changing the base branch). No cubing content.
